editorNote: Lucasfilm takes the game makers’ desk this week, as September’s computer magazines put a new generation of play, exploration and learning under the lamp.
morningLine: This week in 1984: Lucasfilm’s first games claim the cover, while Prince moves to number one.

lead.headline: Lucasfilm Brings Movie-Scale Worlds to the Game Screen
lead.dek: Rescue on Fractalus and Ballblazer give Atari players two sharply different visions of computer play.
body: September’s Electronic Games puts the first Lucasfilm–Atari games on its cover and asks whether filmmakers can make games worth playing. Its answer is emphatic: Rescue on Fractalus and Ballblazer bring the studio’s eye for spectacle to the Atari home-computer screen. The magazine describes a design group led by Stephen D. Arnold and Peter S. Langston, with David Fox guiding the rescue game.

In Rescue on Fractalus, the pilot skims a hostile planet in search of stranded flyers. The instruments sit beneath a broad forward view; a rescued spaceman runs to the craft and knocks before the player opens the airlock. Such small actions, the designers tell Electronic Games, are meant to sustain the illusion of a mission rather than interrupt it with an abstract score chase.

The landscape is more than scenery. Lucasfilm’s team adapted fractal-geometry ideas so that mountains and valleys form a consistent terrain: fly between two peaks, turn around and the geography is still there. The effect gives a home-computer screen the scale of a place to explore, not merely a succession of painted backdrops.

Ballblazer takes the other route, turning futuristic sport into a swift, competitive contest. Together the titles make an unusually confident first pair for a new game label. The September article documents their contemporary reception; it should not be read as claiming that both games first reached every retail shelf during this particular week.

stories.headline: Seven Cities of Gold Makes the Map the Adventure
body: September’s COMPUTE! review finds Electronic Arts and Ozark Softscape sending players from Spain across an ocean whose dangers begin with provisions and navigation. In The Seven Cities of Gold, ships, crew and supplies have to be managed before an expedition can discover a shore.

The reviewer describes a game with more than 2,800 screens and a utility that can generate new continents. Trade, exploration and the decision to return home shape a voyage far more open-ended than a fixed arcade course. The Atari edition is listed at $39.95; the review says a Commodore 64 edition is coming soon.

stories.headline: Ultima III Packs a Whole Campaign into a Box
body: COMPUTE! calls Exodus: Ultima III a fantasy role-playing standout in its September review. The Commodore 64 player forms a party of up to four characters, with professions, attributes and spell books to consider before setting out across Sosaria.

A cloth map, guides and magic books make the $59.95 package feel like a tabletop campaign transported to disk. The review praises the plot, color and sound while noting that repeated combat can slow the journey. It is a contemporary review, not a claim of a release this week.

stories.headline: Educational Software Claims More of the Home Screen
body: A September COMPUTE! package is devoted to the educational-software boom, from advice on choosing a title to new trends in learning. The magazine’s prominent treatment is a sign that the home computer is being sold as a study tool as well as a game machine.

That promise still requires judgment at the counter. COMPUTE!’s companion pieces ask readers to examine how a program teaches, rather than trust an educational label on the carton. Its issue also includes the named learning programs The Tester and Missile Math.

stories.headline: The Modem Buyer Meets the Telephone Line
body: A reader in September’s COMPUTE! asks whether a modem needs a rotary phone or will work with Touch-Tone. The magazine replies that most modems work with both, and points to the Commodore 1650 as an auto-dial model that can emulate rotary dialing.

It is a small question with a large implication: going online is becoming an ordinary home-computer purchase, but compatibility between the computer, modem and telephone service is still part of the shopping list. The editors advise checking a dealer or manufacturer before buying.
